usually been split in two periods of ten minutes each. But the time allotment is 20 minutes.
With respect to the matter mentioned by the minister relating to whether or not he would have to seek from members of his own party time out of their allotment of time in which to respond, that is not correct. It is not an allocation of time to a party. It is an individual member's allocation of time.
If I understand what the minister is suggesting, then possibly a member from his side of the House might give up some of his time in order that the minister may answer. I do not know how it could be worked out mechanically. It can certainly be done with a little planning in advance, if the Chair is advised and the House is made aware of the arrangement. It has been done previously over the past couple of days.
I also realize that the minister is attempting to solve the problem that occurs when he is asked a series of questions but is unable to respond because the allotted time of the questioner has expired. I do not have an answer to that problem. The minister makes what seems to me to be a good point, that perhaps there is a problem with procedure in that regard, but it is the procedure with which we are working at the moment. I can only say that hon. members have now heard the minister's comments on that problem and presumably members who choose to use their entire 20 minutes will be aware that even if they do ask questions they will not obtain an answer if the 20 minutes have expired.
I go back to the other aspect and say that if the minister wishes to make arrangements with other members of his own party, the House has not objected to this procedure in previous sittings in this Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Chairman, I was one of the hon. members who objected to the minister having the time to answer the hon. member for Elgin, and it was based on my experience in this committee during discussion on the transportation estimates. An hon. member is allotted 20 minutes and he can use that time in any way he sees fit. The minister should realize that his own parliamentary secretary also spoke for 20 minutes, and if it was important enough for him to make some comments on the comments of the hon. member for Elgin, he certainly could have used part of the 20 minutes allotted to his parliamentary secretary or, for that matter, used the entire 20 minutes.
The only way in which this committee can operate properly is if we all adhere to the 20 minute time limit. For example, as the next member to speak from our party I intend to ask questions of the minister. In this way hopefully we can have an exchange with regard to some of the various areas in which I am particularly interested.

Mr. Chairman, much can be said for this matter on both sides. Yesterday during the Employment and Immigration estimates, several Liberal members used their 20 minutes to make a speech. That is their right, but the purpose of this exercise is to obtain information from the ministers. I

December 9, 1980
Supply
would also suggest that sometimes the minister, by reminiscing and taking a long time to answer, wastes our time as well.

Mr. Chairman, may I say briefly that the system seemed to work fairly well during the last four days. Each member who gets the floor is allowed 20 minutes, and he has the right to use the full 20 minutes or he can speak briefly and leave time for questions. If the minister will be patient, I am sure he will have plenty of time to answer questions as the committee proceeds.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: If there was a point of order in terms of an appeal to the Standing Orders, 1 do not think it is necessary to pursue the matter any further. In any event, I recognize that the minister has somewhat of a difficult point and that he might, by consultation with the members of his own party, be able to resolve that point with a shuffle in the time arrangement.
Mr. Chairman, which side of the House will speak next?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Lisgar will be the next speaker. As is the custom during normal debate on a bill, the Chair recognizes alternately members from the left and the right. There is a proportion as between members of the three parties which is hopefully adhered to. May I now recognize the hon. member for Lisgar.

Mr. Chairman, at the outset I would like to correct the impression which the Minister of Agriculture has left with regard to agricultural research. I do not believe that the minister meant to leave the impression that he or his government increased the research budget in the main estimates which were being discussed earlier. Those main estimates were prepared by the former Progressive Conservative government, and in that context the research portion was allocated before he became the Minister of Agriculture once again.
My first question centres on the area of grain and grain exports. It has been my understanding, since I became a member of Parliament in the early seventies, that if it was not for grain and oil seeds Canada's agricultural picture would not be very rosy. These two grains are the basic export thrust of our country. They make the balance of trade picture in agriculture look very good.
As the minister knows, or should know, world trade in grains and oil seeds has more than doubled. The United States has benefited mostly from this statistic. Since 1961 their exports have tripled and their share has grown from 48 per cent to some 59 per cent. Canada, Australia and Argentina have slipped from 31 per cent to 25 per cent over that same 20 year period from the early 1960s to 1980. This would indicate that we have a long way to go in encouraging and increasing our agricultural exports.
A good many people in this country, particularly in western Canada, are vitally concerned over this drop and the fact that we have not been able to move back up to the level of exports
which we enjoyed in the early 1970s. There has been some discussion, most recently by the Canadian Wheat Board Advisory Committee, on what has been called an assured marketing system. If what I know about this assured marketing system is correct, it would mean that the Canadian Wheat Board would purchase all the grain at the end of the crop year at the initial price on the farm. What would happen then-for example, perhaps they would simply lock the bin-has not yet been worked out.
I am surprised that the bureaucracy in Ottawa would be considering this idea at this time when the government is low on cash. While I thought they would listen to the proposal, I did not think any action would be taken. It is my understanding that this approach is being considered and that the cost figure which is being mentioned is upwards of $.5 billion in terms of maximum expenses if the program went ahead.
My question to the minister is this. How closely is this approach being considered by either the minister's department or by the grain group? Would the minister also comment on whether or not there will be any studies on this particular program? If my memory serves me correctly, the Wheat Board Advisory Committee wants some kind of decision on this particular program by the start of the 1981 crop year. I believe it was Roy Atkinson of Saskatoon who put the matter forward. Would the minister comment?

Mr. Chairman, I am not aware of what the hon. member is discussing. Is he talking about feed grain or wheat? The Wheat Board Advisory Committee and the Canadian Livestock Feed Board Advisory Committee met and recommended that the Canadian Wheat Board take over total control of all feed grains.
That is right.

That was a recommendation they made in case no other system could be devised to provide equity in the feed grain system. I do not know what is going to come of that, but I think it is great that these two groups met to discuss a problem which they recognized. The Wheat Board and the Canadian Livestock Feed Board would have to give the matter some consideration, and then it would have to come to the government for further consideration before it could be approved. It is only about a month since the two groups made that recommendation so I do not think there has been detailed study of it.

Mr. Chairman, even if the Canadian Wheat Board advisory committee and the Canadian Livestock Feed Board are both considering this matter and make a recommendation, obviously the program will come to nothing if the federal government has not studied it. Does the minister know if his department or the grains group propose to study the matter so that they will have their own information available?

Mr. Chairman, many of the farm organizations have made suggestions about how the feed grain system
December 9, 1980

should operate. This is one such suggestion from two different groups, and I must answer that we are continually reviewing the program and it is under concentrated review at the present time.
It may be of interest to the hon. member to know that I received an advance copy of the agriculture report of the Canada West Foundation the other day which stated that this should all come under the Canadian Wheat Board, or else be on the open, free market-that it should not be half and half. That is another suggestion.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to get drawn into a philosophical discussion of what should or should not come under the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board. I assume from the minister's answer that there is a study which will be released in due course. I suppose the government will then decide whether there is any financial or other justification for this fairly major shift that would obviously have to be taken at substantial cost to the government.
My second question is one that was raised at an agriculture committee meeting some time ago, about the grain embargo. To all intents and purposes the embargo is finished, although it is sometimes difficult to know that from what the minister responsible for the Wheat Board says when he makes statements in connection with it. It has been said that the money going to western farmers would be in the neighbourhood of $60 million to $80 million. It has also been said that the money would be paid, if not before the end of December, then at least sometime in January.
Can the minister confirm whether the figure of $60 million to $80 million is accurate, and whether the moneys will be paid out to the farmer as promised by the government, in the month of December or in January?

Mr. Chairman, if I understood correctly, the hon. member has two questions. The First one is whether the embargo is over. 1 believe 1 should say it is because we are back to normal trading with the U.S.S.R.
The second question is whether there will be compensation for farmers who lost income because of the embargo. That remains to be seen, Mr. Chairman. The final report has yet to be submitted, and 1 hope this will take place within a few days. When it is, I shall make a submission. I cannot tell the hon. member at this time how many millions of dollars will be involved, it must be fulfilled. We picked up the commitment from the previous government that compensation would be paid to farmers for the commodities under embargo. I have not been informed that this commitment will not be fulfilled.

Mr. Chairman, I have another question concerning grains, something that has annoyed many farmers in western Canada. This particular matter is over and done with, but I would be interested to know whether it could happen again. Apparently Ontario has been buying barley from the Canadian Wheat Board at a price much lower than that on the world market at the time of purchase, and has been selling its own barley at the higher world market price. One hears about
Supply
western alienation, Mr. Chairman, and it is little things like this that contribute to that feeling.
Last Thursday I attended a meeting of 300 farmers in Manitoba when this matter was brought up. There is not a lot of money involved, but the principle is important. They are willing to sell their barley to Ontario, but when Ontario farmers then sell their own barley on the offshore market at a higher price, they begin to wonder what kind of country they are living in. 1 understand that the Canadian Wheat Board was not in favour of this action but was overruled either by political pressure or by the minister.
As I said, there is not a lot of money involved as only about 800,000 bushels of barley were sold, but if this symbolic gesture were made in some other part of the country, say, Ontario or Quebec, 1 know it would give rise to the same kind of problem. From a western point of view it does not seem right. I would ask the minister to comment on this matter and I would urge him most strongly not to allow this type of thing to happen again.

Mr. Chairman, the Ontario barley sale that the hon. member refers to normally takes place over a period of five or six years. It is true that a permit was issued by the Canadian Wheat Board after an order in council was passed. I was not in Canada at the time. One of the hon. members' colleagues mentioned that I was in China. I was not involved in this action but I was fully aware of it before I left, and it appeared to me to be a normal sale. The permit was for 30,000 tons, and 15,000 tons were accumulated on order, to be delivered. I understand that it just left the country within the last week.
If I had anything to do with this sort of thing again, Mr. Chairman, I can tell the hon. member that I would not take the same action. I received strong representations from the ministry of agriculture in Ontario on behalf of the barley producers of Ontario who normally made these sales, that it was hurting their market. It should be understood that the barley produced in Ontario always sells at $20 to $30 per ton below western barley. A different pricing structure governs it, although 1 do not know why that is.
It burns me that the people who sold that barley-one is a multinational-probably made more money on the sale of that barley than farmers made in three or four years by producing a ton of barley. Yet all it took was a scratch of a pen. That annoys me more than anything and it is why I would never make representations for them again. The Ontario ministry of agriculture asked us to make the representation to the Wheat Board and the Government of Canada that it was important that these barley sales be made. The barley is produced in the New Liskeard area and other parts of Ontario, and has always been sold to a commercial market which they wanted again this year. The permit was issued for 30,000 tons and they accumulated approximately 15,000 tons, which was loaded recently on two different boats.
The hon. member intimated that the Wheat Board supplied the barley. Mr. Chairman, the Wheat Board has not supplied

December 9, 1980
Adjournment Motion
barley to eastern Canada for domestic consumption since last April. The barley that was supplied was offboard barley that producers can supply or not as they like. The vast bulk of the barley consumed in the last five years was offboard barley because of the price structure decided upon by the Chicago corn competitive price that they use. That has been to the advantage of barley producers for a couple of years since that program has been in effect. However, it can work both ways. It rarely works to the advantage of producers. Mostly it works to their disadvantage. That must be changed. All I am saying is that is has been blown way out of proportion.
There is another thing about which not much has been said. I am speaking about long-term barley sales which are made three years ahead. The buyer makes as much as a 100 per cent capital gain on that. People will not ask for compensation for that. I am suggesting that the Canadian Livestock Feed Board, on behalf of the producers in British Columbia and eastern Canada who use barley, make the same kind of long-term agreement to barley, perhaps three years or perhaps five years. If a 100 per cent profit is made, no one will say anything. I say treat them the same way as any farm buyer of barley, but make them sign that kind of a contract so that barley producers in western Canada will know what they will receive and the eastern person who is producing that product, meat, pork or beef, is in a better position to provide more stability to the production entity for the consuming public in Canada, at the same time. This is especially true with commodities on cost-price formulae. It is very easy to forecast a year ahead, under those kinds of programs, approximately what the cost of production will be.

Mr. Chairman, there are about two minutes remaining. I have a brief question for the minister. When does he anticipate an increase, hopefully in the $2 range, in the initial price for wheat? Will it be before the end of December or after?

Mr. Chairman, if I go by what western producers tell me, they want an increase, but not before January 2. I have been to many meetings, as one member has already mentioned. An increase is wanted, but not before the end of the year. Western producers want this increase in the new year, starting in January. I think at that time it will be considered.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: Order, please. Before I recognize the next hon. member, may I deal with the proceedings tonight. It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 40, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie)-The Canadian economy-Tax incentives for industry locating in slow growth areas; the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster)-National Revenue- Income tax deductions from wages of spouses in unincorporated businesses; the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revel-stoke (Mr. Parker)-Northern pipelines-Expropriation of land in British Columbia.

The House resumed consideration in committee of Bill C-47, for granting to Her Majesty certain sums of money for the Government of Canada for the financial year ending March 31, 1981-Mr. Pinard-Mr. Blaker in the chair. DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
Vote No. 1

Mr. Chairman, I am happy to join my colleagues in bringing my humble contribution to the debate on the estimates of Agriculture Canada.
Recently, Mr. Chairman, I had the pleasure of meeting one of the directors of the dairy producers' federation of Mauricie. He gave me a message to convey saying, as soon as you get a chance to speak to the minister, do congratulate him on his current dairy policy. Now, Mr. Minister, those were the very people who, in 1976, came here to the Hill and tried to disguise you into a snowman by throwing powdered milk at you. Mr. Minister, you know the courage of those good old farmers. And they also can appreciate gallant people like you for, at the time, it took courage on your part to take over control of the dairy production, knowing full well that the decision was politically disastrous, but knowing also that it would benefit Canadian dairy producers as a group.
Mr. Minister, you showed foresight then and 1 am happy to see that dairy producers rejoice today and pay you this tribute. A giant step has been made in the last ten years toward recognizing the value of the farmer and ensuring him the standard of living he deserves. Still, that is no reason for reducing the assistance the department gives that group of the agricultural sector.
Mr. Minister, rumours have it that Treasury Board intends to cancel the $2.66 per hundredweight subsidy paid to dairy producers. If expenditures must be cut, it can be done in many other places without attacking dairy producers. I beg of you,
December 9, 1980

Mr. Minister, do not allow Treasury Board to slash your budget. I know you as a fighter and I am sure you will be able to convince the members of the cabinet, and that you will not let them push you around. Moreover, you may rest assured that I will support you if you need soldiers and that all hon. members representing rural ridings such as mine will also rally behind you, for if these subsidies were automatically cut off, we would be faced with an increase in inflationary forces which are our common enemy. Should these subsidies be cut off, the prices of butter and powdered milk would rise by at least 30 cents and anywhere between 15 and 20 cents a pound respectively. I should like to pause now, Mr. Minister, so that you may tell me what you think and whether these rumours are founded.

Mr. Chairman, I have no knowledge whatever of any such recommendation. One of the hon. member's constituents has made a comment about the minister being a fighter. That would be something to make me fighting mad. I believe we have the best dairy program of any country in the world. It is a healthy program and one of the best managed programs in the world. It is under review. It is a program I agreed to, and I know of no such recommendations whatever.
[ Translation]

Mr. Chairman, I am concerned about something else. I am referring to the financial assistance provided to our young farmers who want to purchase land. The whole rural community is aware that under the Farm Credit Act, they can borrow up to 100 per cent of the total value of the livestock, lands and buildings. But you know that to operate a dairy farm, they also need quotas the value of which often exceeds $50,000. What happens, therefore, is that young farmers can purchase the land and equipment they need under the Farm Credit Act, but the Farm Credit Corporation does not recognize the value of the quota as a guarantee for the loan. It means that young farmers must pay some money that many have not and consequently they cannot fulfil their wishes and take up farming as the trade of their choice.
Canada now has specialized agents in the sale of agricultural farms travelling through the country to find lands for Europeans who would like to settle in Canada, namely Belgian, Swiss or Dutch people. I have nothing against those people who arrive in Canada loaded with money and purchase our lands with thousands or millions. I am even pleased to see that Canadian farmers selling their lands for a good price. However, this is the reason why I disagree. I do not see why the sons of our farmers cannot obtain the necessary assistance to carry on and till the land which our forefathers have cleared without being bound to leave our heritage to foreigners due to lack of money or government assistance. I would like the minister to tell me whether he is considering the possibility of increasing the funds earmarked for the Farm Credit Corporation.
Supply

Mr. Chairman, with regard to the lending policy of the Farm Credit Corporation, the amount of capital it requires is presently under review. No matter what is done federally, we cannot provide all the equity needed in the agricultural industry. Even though 74 per cent of loans is made to farmers between the ages of 17 and 35, more money is needed in the Farm Credit Corporation.
Inequity in the agricultural industry is increasing more than one would imagine, especially in those provinces which have so much money they do not know what to do with it. For instance, in Alberta a young farmer can borrow at 6 per cent interest. He has a tremendous advantage over someone producing the same product in Manitoba, Ontario or Quebec and competing for the domestic or international market. I repeat that we are reviewing the Farm Credit Corporation.
With regard to quotas, this is a provincially run program. This adds a tremendous cost to young farmers becoming involved in farming. Something must be done not only with regard to dairy quotas, but turkey quotas, and in fact any quota with a value on it. This should be reviewed.
There is little action I can take other than to see the national marketing programs continue. We must try to squash such things as companies accumulating quotas. That is not my idea of a national marketing agency, provincial marketing board or a joint national marketing agency in order to preserve the Canadian family farm. Although it has not reached a dangerous position, it is gradually creeping toward that.

Mr. Chairman, the same problem comes up every year at this time, especially in the cheese industry. During the year, this industry helps to dispose of dairy products which would otherwise be considered surpluses which the Canadian Dairy Commission would have to purchase. These cheese dairies, two of which I visited recently, are now short of milk. Those who are able to get large quantities of milk during the summer produce and store their products and pay for storage from their own income.
Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether it would be possible for department officials to find a way to encourage dairy producers to produce as much during the winter as during the summer, as this would be the ideal solution in my opinion. I know we have had and still have several programs to encourage dairy producers to produce as much in the winter as in the summer. However, with the subsidies we now give to dairy producers, we could perhaps find a system which would stimulate producers to produce during the winter, which would certainly solve the problem. I do not know whether the minister and his officials have tried to find a solution, but I believe it would be greatly appreciated by the industry if some program could be developed. I await the reply of the minister.

December 9, 1980
Supply

Mr. Chairman, the whole dairy program is geared to producers who produce 12 months of the year. 1 do not have the figures with me at this time, but there is an amazing number of farmers who produce 12 months of the year, producing high quality fresh milk for the dairies and the cheese factories. Production of our specialty cheeses and other cheeses has increased tremendously because of this factor. Some regions of Canada, possibly because of climatic conditions, are not doing this, but they may not have the processing facilities geared to that kind of production. We would like to see close to if not 100 per cent of our dairy producers producing 12 months of the year. Our cost-price formula is geared toward 12-month production, not seven or eight months.

Mr. Minister, I would like to touch briefly on one of the answers you gave my colleague from Lisgar. You were mentioning that Ontario barley always sells on the world market below the price of western barley. The point my colleague was making is it is now selling higher than western barley going into the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
1 would like to take up something else you said. You mentioned that the corn competitive formula causes some anomalies and it will have to be changed. I think 1 understood your correctly. If so, I would like your comments. I will take a little longer so that you can think while you are sitting there rather than while you are standing, which would only take up extra time.
A statement was made by you to the Quebec Farmers' Association in Quebec. I quote:
The "Crowsnest rate" and the feed freight assistance program have reduced the cost of grain shipped into Quebec and thus lowered the cost of producing hogs and poultry here. These subsidies have resulted in benefits for western grain growers, but they have also decreased the natural comparative advantage for livestock production on the prairies and given assistance to livestock producers in the east.
Also, the "Crowsnest rate" has favoured the growth in Quebec of processing plants for meat, flour and vegetable oils since products processed in the west are not eligible for the preferential statutory rate, while the raw products are.
Because of that statement I would like to ask about some statements made by your colleagues. The Minister of Transport called for a task force to study the Crow rate. The disorderly senator in the other place said there will be no change in the Crow for some time. You, Mr. Minister, said you are sick and tired of studies and committees on western transportation problems and there will be no more. Does this mean you are going to stay with the status quo and deprive the people of western Canada of the natural advantage to the other provinces in Canada, are you going to go along with the Minister of Transport in his supposition, or with the disorderly minister from the other place?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. The atmosphere in Committee of the Whole is more relaxed. It is quite common for members and ministers to address each other directly. It is the responsibility of the Chair to remind hon. members that it is preferable and in accordance with the rules
if they address one another through the Chair. In other words, when speaking of another member, the reference is "the hon. member has said", rather than "you".
Second, whatever style of debate we may accept, it might be wise to leave the members of the other place, who do not have an opportunity to defend themselves in this place, without reference to "disorderly". It may not be the best form. I do not say that it is out of order. I just want to note that it could be a small problem the hon. member might consider, because this might go on for days.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to bring to the attention of the hon. member that I was talking about domestic barley prices producers received in Ontario. As history will show, they are always lower than what a western producer receives for barley or what it would cost to have western barley put into that area. There is a discrepancy there. I never said what it sold at, at world price, because I do not know, and I cannot find out what the traders were able to accumulate as a profit. I am told that if a profit was made it was not passed on to any of the producers.
If the traders made an unwarranted mark-up on it, this is the kind of thing that makes one angry. I am sure the hon. member's party condones this great multinational type of operation and this type of world sales program. When we talk about some of the Canadian Wheat Board operations, the hon. member may have some reservations about it. I have talked with him in private conversation and he has told me whom he supported as far as marketing grain was concerned.
I said if we were going to do anything about the Crow rates, and something must be done about them, then it had to be fair for our grain producers so they would not be put at a disadvantage with any other group of grain producers with whom they compete. It must be that kind of system we develop. I did not say it should not be touched or changed. It should be changed.
My colleague, the Minister of Transport, has the right to say "task force" if he wants. I was not aware he was suggesting a task force when I was questioned about that in western Canada this past week. We have volumes and volumes of studies on rail transportation, Crow rates, and what should be done and should not be done. There may be an interdepartmental group looking at it, and if that is the case I am in favour of that kind of task force. This way it may be done quickly and a solution reached.
I mentioned before that the livestock producer and the grain producer in Canada, in some way, must come to realize how important it is to both of them that they survive. If the hon. member wants to read some of my old speeches, he may do so. They were before his time in this House of Commons. When I was in western Canada I said they were dependent on one another.
Eighty per cent of the feed grain produced in Canada is consumed in Canada. The biggest customer for a feed grain producer is the Canadian livestock-poultry producer. If I were a grain producer I would make sure my biggest customer was
December 9, 1980

looked after the best, and then take care of the other 20 per cent. Some years they buy and some years they do not buy. The livestock producers, be they in the east or the west, are the best consumers and the best users of domestic feed grain produced in Canada and should be well looked after. For instance, the freight rate structure and those types of things should encourage, the processing of those products produced in western Canada. It was pointed out earlier, and I have admitted, that some of the freight structures were not that fair so as to encourage this processing. It was fair to the grain producer but not to the livestock producer in western Canada.

Mr. Chairman, regarding the compensation which is due and is just to the producers of western Canada, and indeed all of Canada, because of the embargo imposed on sales to the Soviet Union-the suggestion was made by the hon. minister-it is his hope that the higher prices farmers would receive this year would make up for the lack of money they lost due to the embargo. Eligher grain prices, of course, will not make up for the lower prices caused by the embargo. The two are entirely separate issues. Elave the producers of western Canada been set up by an answer given to my hon. friend and colleague from Vegreville to a question posed to the Minister of Transport who is responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board? The hon. member for Vegreville asked, and 1 quote:
Does the minister feel that more than the embargo limit of 3.8 million tonnes of grain could have been sold and delivered to the U.S.S.R. in the last crop year and. if so, on what does he base his assumption?
The answer to that question quoted from Hansard is no. Because we could not have sold more grain according to the Minister of Transport, and the Minister of Agriculture is saying he believes there should be compensation payable, can the Minister of Agriculture indicate whether there is a difference of opinion, or is it one way the minister and this government are seeking of moving aside a little from the commitment made by the past government and which this government has accepted?
Regarding the feed grain policy, 1 would like to recall a comment made by my colleague from Lisgar, and some statements made by advisory committees to the Canadian Wheat Board and to the Canadian Livestock Feed Board. The advisory committee to the Canadian Livestock Feed Board is not an advisory committee to the minister. The advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board, I would assume, is not an advisory committee to the minister. On the point of supposedly unanimous support given to the proposal that all feed grain should be placed under the Canadian Wheat Board, I have information here which tells me at least four members of the advisory committee to the Wheat Board were not in favour of this proposal.
While we are talking about the cost of feed grains in our country today, I should like to quote an article from the Saskatchewan Natural Products Marketing Council publication in the province of Saskatchewan. It begins by criticizing the open market system, saying that:
Supply
In this study we use the street price for feed wheat, oats and barley quoted by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool for a 25-cent/cwt freight zone.
Further on it says:
Since August 1, 1974, the private grain trade has been permitted to buy feed grains on the prairies-
And that includes all the pools, and all the line companies.
The publication goes on:
Prairie grain producers have always felt that western grains should be marketed in the most efficient manner possible, and... reflect the actual charges (justifiable cost) of handling, transporting and marketing the grain.
It also makes mention of the fact that elevator companies have charged an excess profit margin, and this is using Saskatchewan Wheat Pool statistics from the province of Saskatchewan, on feed wheats of 24 cents per bushel, on oats of .07 cents per bushel, and on barley of .04 cents per bushel.
I would just like the minister's thoughts as to the cause of some of this excess profit which has been collected by all elevator companies because of the open marketing system.
I would like to give the minister one more statistic which was released on Friday, October 31, 1980. The price for 3 CW feed wheat export in store at Thunder Bay was $251.12 per tonne. For the same wheat, domestic feed Thunder Bay, the price was $175.80. That is a $75 a tonne difference in what we are asking for export wheat and what we are asking for the same wheat for domestic consumption. 1 would like the minister's comments on that, and I would like to know if he feels that the corn competitive formula has anything to do with this process.
Mr. Chairman, the question asked by the hon. member is technical. I do not have that information before me, but 1 should have it after supper, and I should be able to report to him at that time.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to move to another topic. There has been much discussion, and I believe the minister announced that there will be a statement on the regulation of 2,4-D and MCPA before seeding as to whether they will be removed from the market or further regulated.
In spite of the precautions which have been taken with respect to 2,4-D, no health problems have been documented scientifically. In the province of Saskatchewan we grow about 17 million acres of wheat in a normal year. About 75 per cent of that wheat is sprayed for broadleaf weeds in any given year. Of those 17 million acres about 15 million acres are sprayed with 2,4-D. If 2,4-D is removed from the market, food production in Canada, worth about $10 billion a year of which $6 billion is exported-which is 12 per cent of our total accounts payable-will be lost.
I would like the minister to answer these questions. What chemicals would be available to replace 2,4-D, and at what cost? I am referring to 2,4-D or its counterpart MCPA. Which of the weeds which have all but disappeared would return? How would farmers' yields and incomes be affected and

December 9, 1980
Supply
how would total farm production and, ultimately, export sales be affected?

Mr. Chairman, it is because of dioxins that we are concerned about 2,4-D. There are approximately 1,000 types of dioxins. Only three are possibly deadly. We have to isolate them. We have to make sure we know which ones they are. We are undertaking all the scientific studies and chemical studies which can be made at this time. I do not think 1 should just ban 2,4-D or ask that it be banned. We work closely with my colleagues in the Department of the Environment and the Department of National Health and Welfare because of the good that 2,4-D does,
I agree with the hon. member that farming could not be carried on without some other type of material if 2,4-D were not available. We could not ban 2,4-D just like that and still expect the type of production from farmers we are getting at the present time. We could not expect there to be the production of cereal grains, corn and many other crops which we see today. Some people suggest that we should ban 2,4-D. It is like saying that because there are one thousand varieties of spiders but only three poisonous varieties, we should kill all one thousand varieties to make sure we get the three poisonous ones. I do not intend to recommend that with respect to 2,4-D.
The hon. member made some suggestion that we were trying to get out of paying even if there was reason to pay compensation for farmers' lost income. I did mention that farmers had received higher prices for their grain. I did mention earlier today that some farmers said that they do not want initial payments before January 1. They told me that in Tisdale, the Battlefords, Saskatoon, Regina, Ste. Rose, Dauphin and Morris, and I can think of many other places. They told me that in Lethbridge too. If the final tabulation of the whole grain sales system shows that we owe farmers money-this pertains not just to western farmers because there could be some farmers in eastern Canada who are commercial grain growers also and who are also involved-I do not feel this government would be in a position to say no. We could not welsh on a commitment we have made, so no matter how anyone tries to interpret anything I have said, 1 never intended to say we would welsh on a commitment we made.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the minister's remarks with respect to the chemical 2,4-D. I know he understands how important it is and that if there happens to be something wrong with 2,4-D and there is no substitute, the farmers of western Canada and, indeed, in all of Canada would be in deep trouble.
I am not too sure what the Eddy Arnold song about places in western Canada the minister has visited had to do with my question.
Hank Snow.

I was out in Tisdale too, and we had a little more success in Tisdale than the minister.
I would like to go on to the Farm Credit Corporation. Last year approximately 20,000 farmers approached the Farm Credit Corporation for assistance. Those approaches are documented. There were probably many more who did not fill out application forms, but only 5,700 transactions were completed last year. That was last year, and as a result of a shortage of funds in the Farm Credit Corporation it is forecast that this year 1,000 fewer farmers will be receiving funds. Would the minister explain to the House the steps he has taken to broaden the base of farm credit?
In the estimates there are approximately $16.8 million for emergency assistance to prairie livestock producers affected by drought. I recall some press releases in June and July in which the federal government committed about $67 million for drought assistance. I would like the minister to tell me how much has been paid out to date and how much will be paid out.

Mr. Chairman, we have said how much we have estimated. We have never been conservative in our estimates. We have always been quite liberal, and we have never had to use all the funds. For instance, we set aside $7 million for transportation. We used only close to $6 million for transportation. That was arranged with the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba for the transportation of forage for livestock. There was a meeting yesterday morning. It appears we will be spending very close to $67 million both on forage aid and on the herd maintenance program. The herd maintenance program is under the PFRA which is under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. That agency is administering the herd maintenance program through the people who administer community pastures and that type of program.
However, it appears that it has been well received. I believe
35,000	applications are being processed at the present time under the herd maintenance program. I am going by memory again, but I believe more applications have been received under the forage assistance program in the last two weeks than in the previous two months, so it appears that farmers now have more time to fill out applications. However, they are being processed. Review boards are set up immediately for applicants who feel they are not being dealt with properly. Applicants who have been turned down will have a review board to appeal before. We hope that many of these claims will be settled before the end of the year. I believe that approximately 9,000 have been settled already under the herd maintenance program and probably a couple of thousand under the forage aid program. They are speeding along as fast as they can, but they hope that in the new year, in January, many of these claims will be settled.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all, perhaps 1 should put into perspective some facts that are misinterpreted or miscontrued by the misinformed. Perhaps I should put on record, before going further, the fact that last year gross farm receipts in Canada amounted to $13.9 billion and our exports
December 9, 1980

amounted to $6.1 billion. This would indicate that Canadians paid something like $7.8 billion to the farmers for food produced and consumed in Canada. Now if we were to divide $7.8 billion by 24 million Canadians, we would find that, on an average, each consumer paid $326.65 per year, or 89 cents per day. If we assume that we eat three meals per day, the Canadian consumer paid the Canadian farmer 29.8 cents per meal for food produced and consumed in Canada.
In fact, a recent survey of the cost of a 21-item food basket, in U.S. funds, shows that Canada has the lowest priced food of any of the following countries, in this order: the United States, Australia, the United Kingdom, Spain, Italy, The Netherlands, West Germany, Argentina, Denmark and Japan. The closest of these for similar items was $58.02 for the United States, compared to $55.58 for Canada, and the highest was Japan at $135.10 for the same food basket.
It alarms me, Mr. Chairman, when I read about a consumer spokesperson who recently assailed the farm producing sector and indicated that the consumers were suspicious of our marketing boards. Yet after having made this charge, she admitted, without doing any research, that she believed the return to food producers was equal to that realized in other industries. Of course, she did not say whether she was referring to the Chrysler Corporation, Massey Ferguson or Imperial Oil, nor did she mention the surveys of the USDA food basket report to which I referred earlier, or the report by Mr. A. Cayer released in November, 1979, on the egg industry in Canada, in which he states in conclusion, at page 77, that:
Consumers in Toronto have paid less for eggs than their counterparts in New York, since the implementation of central pricing by CEMA.
Mr. Cayer goes on to point out that:
Analyses carried out by a number of groups over the past five years have been misleading because their use of selective indicators did not adequately reflect the longer-term trends or the significant fluctuations in currency values or in the industry.
Now if this consumer were sincere and well informed, she would have pointed out that in November the retail price of beef increased to $2.64 per pound, and the farm price dropped by 4 cents per pound. This meant an increased spread of 15 cents per pound between the producer and the consumer in one month. In Ontario the retail value of the OFA food basket was $39.69, up $5.48 from November, 1979, or an increase in the farm retail spread of 19 per cent in one year. The farm retail spread is the cost to the consumer of processing, packaging, distributing and merchandising food.
This same consumer spokesperson wondered if farmers were using up the organic matter in the soil or damaging the land by the weight of large machinery. Here again the weight of large machinery has nothing to do with the organic content in the soil. The loss of organic matter in the soil is usually caused by poor soil management or improper crop rotation, not by compaction. In fact, as equipment has become larger and heavier, the size of the tires has increased, resulting in better flotation. It is easier to understand this when we realize that whereas one Canadian farmer could feed five other persons not too many years ago, he can now feed upward of 70. Our
Supply
Canadian agricultural industry is the most efficient in the world.
I will never cease to be amazed, Mr. Chairman, that we allow food into Canada which could just as well be grown domestically. In fact, we import almost $2 billion worth of food which could well be grown here in Canada. One of the most blatant examples of these imports occurred last summer, when two Ontario supermarkets carried only imported peaches, despite the availability of a bumper crop of Ontario peaches. If the workers in those countries where the imports originated had received wages comparable to those of our own workers, I could accept this competition, but when we are competing against wage rates which are in some cases only half ours, consequently involving a lower standard of living, we must ask ourselves: are we importing cheap food or are we importing unemployment? I could also accept some of these imports if the consumer were actually the benefactor, but in many instances the cheaper imported price serves only to give a wider profit margin to the importer.
Another point that I wish to make in regard to food imported into Canada is that these merchandisers are not usually interested in serving the less populated areas but rather concentrate in the Montreal, Toronto and Windsor corridor or the Vancouver area, leaving Canadian processors to serve the more scattered population, or areas where distribution costs are much higher. Are these imported foods produced under the same environmental restrictions as those applied to our own Canadian producers, and does the chemical content conform to the restrictions applied in Canada for our own producers?
I believe, however, that Canadians have taken this vital part of our economy for granted for too long. The recent drought in western Canada and the southwestern U.S., the lower than expected crop yields in Russia and China, indicate the delicate balance of our world grain supplies. In spite of this situation, our market prices for grain are influenced by one of the most unpredictable pricing systems ever devised; I refer to the speculative futures market which is supposed to be geared to supply and demand.
Last week the price of soya beans, for example, dropped by about $1 a bushel. The reason for this drop was not oversupply and it certainly was not an anticipated increased crop in Brazil, because it is still premature to estimate the success of this crop which was planted a few weeks ago. It was people speculating on the commodity markets, speculating and gambling on the basis of the very food we eat, while people on other continents starve.
Mr. Chairman, we in Canada have a better system, a system which, while it is often the victim of speculators in other countries, resists the efforts of manipulators and ensures a more stable return to producers and fair prices to the consumers. I am convinced that as Canadians we can do much more to produce that $2 billion worth of imported food in Canada. As an example, just last week I had the honour of presiding at the opening of Canada's first peanut plant, and was delighted with the quality and flavour of our first Canadian commercial

December 9, 1980
Supply
crop of peanuts. I can see a tremendous future in this area. I want to commend the Minister of Agriculture and Agriculture Canada for their contribution under their New Crop Development Program and the research which made this project possible. I want to commend them also on the other projects that are on stream.
With regard to increased exports, we can also provide the vehicle which would assist our producers to enter into contracts with other countries wanting to buy food, long-term contracts if possible, providing our producers with the incentive to produce a product, knowing that they can sell it at a profit. Canada is one of the few countries of the world which has the vehicle in place to plan production for specific domestic and export markets. I believe the potential could be one of several billion dollars. Of course the spin-off effects will benefit all of society.
The other area I should like to touch upon is the concern that there may be a world grain shortage a few years hence. We realize how delicate the balance is at the present time. If there is a world grain shortage, a world food shortage could naturally follow. With proper planning and research I am convinced Canada could double its output of protein. It is in this area of research that I commend Agriculture Canada for the work it is doing. In the years that I have been farming, however, 1 have noticed what seems to be a shortening of the summer growing season. Those of us involved in farming operations have adapted accordingly.
I am particularly enthused about one interesting aspect of research, that is, research in the area of photosynthesis or the process whereby a plant converts sunlight through its leaves to protein and energy. If we could speed up this process, we could push back the geographical and climatic barriers which curtail the production of specialized crops in more northerly regions or colder climatic zones, thereby strengthening our potential to increase food production.
There are some questions which I want to ask the minister. First, has the research division of Agriculture Canada been conducting research on photosynthesis with the goal of speeding up the process, and what have the successes been at the present time? Second, in the area of research, can Agriculture Canada forecast world crop conditions with infrared sensing equipment in the summer months, and are they doing any work in the area of measuring solar radiation and its effects on different crops? Third, in keeping with the support of national farm organizations in Canada for the concept of a Canadian agriculture export corporation, did the deputy minister of agriculture discover any unserviced markets for food on his recent trip to Mexico, and what is the potential value of those markets? Last, with respect to the Farm Credit Corporation, is any consideration being given at the present time to making funds available to young farmers who want to become established farmers and, using this as a mechanism to stop the purchase of farm land by foreign owners and absentee landlords? This is a very serious situation in some areas of the nation, and I should like to see it dealt with.
I would appreciate any comments the minister may have in reply to my questions.

Mr. Chairman, the Farm Credit Corporation is an old institution which was set up to assist farmers and members of the community, especially those who had been turned down by some other lending institution. In this First instance, the Farm Credit Corporation was to be a lending establishment of last resort for farmers. It was not to be "the" lending institution. At one time nearly 70 per cent of all loans made to farmers in Canada was under the Farm Credit Corporation; now it is something like 40 to 50 per cent of all loans made to farmers. We still think the Farm Credit Corporation has a place in our society. All the countries with which we compete in agricultural production and markets have tremendous lending associations, Crown corporations or similar organizations which are either funded or administered by the government in some fashion or form.
It is felt by some-but certainly not by myself-that all loans should be provided to farmers from the private sector. It is not my intention to go in that direction. My intention is to reorganize the Farm Credit Corporation to make it into the kind of organization we have always wanted, so that our farmers will be in the position to borrow from a lending institution which has a feeling for the farming and rural community of Canada. We want such a lending institution.
We shall be presenting new legislation to the House concerning amendments to the Farm Credit Corporation early in the new year. I had hoped that it would be before the House of Commons prior to Christmas, but it does not appear that we will have the time.
Dealing with the area of new markets, the deputy minister and a small group recently visited Mexico and Cuba. They, with the Canadian Feed Manufacturer's Association, presented a program in Cuba which showed how to use Canadian feed to its utmost in feeding swine. The mortality rate in Cuban swine was 5.5 per cent, but when Canadian feed was used the mortality rate immediately dropped in weaning pigs to about .3 per cent. So, there is a potential market there for perhaps
200,000	tonnes of feed per year. There is an increased possibility of new markets in Mexico in many new agricultural commodities, different varities of wheat, different dairy products and different oilseed products.
I just want to say that we are very optimistic, because Mexico indicated that it will spend nearly half of its oil earnings on food to upgrade the nutrition and protein intake of its people. If it does that, it will be spending about S20 billion in the next couple of years on agricultural products, and it is up to us to get part of it. We will try to get part of it, and that is what the deputy minister and the group were doing in Mexico.
In the first part of January we will be returning to Mexico to try to ensure that some agreements are signed for the purchase of these products. In some instances our producers may have to change their production for markets which will be long-term in nature. I think a conservative estimate for the
December 9, 1980

first year would be about a $500 million increase in trade in agricultural products with Mexico.
When we talk about in-house research into the use of solar energy, we are increasing research directed toward maximizing the efficiency of breeding for higher yield. The higher priority areas include growth analysis, the rates of accumulating solar energy, the partitioning of photosynthesis, the rate and timing of plant development of nitrogen metabolism. Perhaps we are not doing as much as we would like, but I can assure the hon. member that we are moving in that area because we figure it is a very important one.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock the hon. Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Ferguson) had the floor.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when time was called at six o'clock I had been speaking about some of the excellent research and development being done by Agriculture Canada. If we look at the poultry and livestock sector in Canada we will recognize that one of the biggest turkey hatcheries in North America, with the best breeding stock, is located in my constituency. In the area of laying hens, egg production and broiler production one of the best operations in the world is located in the Cambridge area. We all recognize the standard of excellence which has prevailed in the dairy industry, beef cattle and horse sectors of Canada over the years.
I would like to ask the minister if the present system of parental blood typing, which is being conducted through the Department of Agriculture, will be continued in Canada. We have the best expertise in this field in the world. There was some concern by Canadian livestock breeders that this program might be farmed out to private institutions. Could the minister assure us that this program will be continued.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know how much of this parental blood typing will be carried on. I do know that we will be blood typing horses. The horse breeders of Canada will be paying for it. We do intend to recover the full costs of this project. It will cost the government nothing to do this for the horse breeders. Elorse breeders are asking us to do this. The swine breeders are also asking us for parental blood typing. It
Supply
is a very costly undertaking for us to become involved in. We just do not have provision for it in our budget unless we are to get full recovery. It appears the horse breeders are the group most inclined to go along with this, more so than any other group in the livestock area.
I cannot tell the hon. member any more about it now. We have met with the swine breeders and the sheep breeders. Both groups want this kind of project. The cost per animal subjected to these tests is about $60. For an animal which is only worth two or three times that amount, there is concern about spending that much money. These groups want it done in Canada. We want it done in Canada. If these tests are conducted in some other part of the world, for example the United States of America, the results would be put into their computer systems. The result would be that they would know more about our livestock industry than we would.
We want to continue with this testing but in order to do so we must find a more economical way of doing it in some of the livestock industries.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to speak on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. It gives me a chance to say a few words in support of Canada's number one industry-our agriculture industry. It is an industry of which we are all proud.
I know the Minister of Agriculture feels he is doing a good job. I would be surprised if he thought otherwise. However, all is not well in the agriculture industry in Canada today, and the government must take a large share of the blame. I say that for two reasons, Mr. Chairman. First, the government, through the Department of Agriculture and other agencies, is deeply involved in the private sector of agriculture. For that reason the government should recognize the symptoms of an illness in the industry as quickly as anyone else. Second, the government is not as quick to jump in and help this industry as they were when trouble developed in other sectors, such as the automotive and heavy machinery industries. In fairness to the minister, though, it may be that he does not have the support in cabinet that some of his colleagues seem to have.
The agriculture industry in Canada is facing problems that are serious enough to threaten the very future of food production in our country unless we take steps now to identify them, and then to deal with them. There is a large degree of interrelationship between the problems facing the agriculture industry, just as in other types of industry. But unlike most other industries, the effects on the food industry could be both immediate and long range. Some of these problems are inflation, high cost of production, high cost of good farm land, the lack of ready sources of low cost financing for capital and other operating costs, and uncertainty and instability in the marketplace.
The deadly combination of inflation and high interest rates is driving farmers out of business and making it impossible for many young people to enter the agriculture industry. The

December 9, 1980
Supply
young couple fortunate enough to buy a family farm for reasonable terms will lock themselves into a future in the agricultural industry, but what about those who have to buy on the open market? To put it simply, the average young couple today would not even be in the running for that type of money. More farmers leave the land every year. Some of them get fed up with the low rate of return on their investment and their labour. When that happens many of them look around for a likely buyer, and it is often a developer who plans to take the land out of production.
While 1 am on this subject, I would like to point out that every year tens of thousands of acres of prime agricultural land are taken out of production and used as sites for industries and other non-agricultural purposes. This has the additional effect of pushing up prices of other farms in the area. Other farmers, even if they are hard workers and conscientious, find themselves caught between poor market conditions and high interest rates.
Last year the pork producers were forced to sell hogs at less than production costs. When they looked around for money to restock and weather the poor market season they simply could not afford to go further into debt at today's interest costs. In far too many cases, the farmer cannot turn to any private or government agency for assistance which he can afford. I think many, if not all of them, are waiting for the low interest rates which were promised by the Minister of Agriculture to farmers during the last election campaign. Could this be yet another example of the minister's lack of clout in cabinet?
The decrease in the number of dairy farms in our country is real cause for concern, if not alarm. I think some of my colleagues have given this figure before, but it is worth repeating. This has me deeply concerned, both as a member of Parliament from Ontario, and as a consumer. I do not know how many of those lost farms are in Ontario, but I suspect it is too many.
Between 1971 and 1979 there was a decline in the number of dairy farms in Canada from 129,000 to 70,000, a loss of
59,000	dairy farms in just eight years. In that same period the number of dairy cows and heifers in Ontario declined from 986,300 to 770,000. This leads me to believe that a large number of the farms that were pulled out of the dairy business were in Ontario. Mr. Chairman, to me these are dangerous signs, signs that can no longer be ignored.
It must be admitted that improved production methods and good management resulted in only a slight reduction in milk production in that period, but I am sure there is a limit to the process by which fewer farms and fewer cows can produce the same amount of milk. I believe we are close to that limit, and since the population in Ontario is increasing at a faster rate than that of any other province, the decline in dairy farms and dairy cattle in Ontario concerns me in a more personal way than it does some other hon. members.
I have been told there is some concern in the dairy industry as to what the federal government has in mind with regard to the present national dairy policy. I do not believe the dairy
industry is being given enough information about the government's plans. They want to know and, indeed, they must know whether or not the government plans to make any major changes in the national policy and, if so, what will those changes be? They do not want to know the day or the week before they are brought in, but well in advance. I venture to say that it would be unwise for the government to plan any changes to the dairy policy without consulting the industry.
I would like to get back to interest rates for a moment because there is no question that high interest rates represent the greatest single stumbling block to a healthy agriculture industry. There is no question that this issue will have to be addressed by the minister and his colleagues in cabinet in the immediate future. Interest rates creep into every segment of the industry and it is the smaller farm units that are hit first and hardest by spiralling rates. For instance, the cost of farm marchinery has increased due to inflation. Most farmers are forced to buy machinery on time and when one adds the effect of inflation and high interest rates, one can see that it becomes more and more difficult for small farmers to purchase modern machinery and equipment.
Next to modern, efficient machinery, perhaps the most important single thing to a small farmer is fertilizer. Crop yield and crop quality are vital to any farm operation, and this means judicious use of the right kinds and quantities of fertilizer. Unfortunately, the price of fertilizer has been rising at a rapid rate over the past few years, and this is cutting into the profits of all farm operations. In some cases where farmers cannot absorb these higher costs, they are abandoning the use of chemical fertilizers altogether. I am sure this results in a decrease in yield per acre as well as a decrease in the quality of crop.
These are some of the problems facing the agriculture industry today in Canada, but there are others. I have not touched on the end result of all this investment in money, time and labour. 1 have not mentioned the marketplace. If a farmer does not make it in the marketplace, as the saying goes, he just does not make it. And there are problems in the marketplace in Canada today.
In many respects it is a case of feast or famine. For example, we are all familiar with the plight of potato farmers last year and the year before. Last year potato producers took a real beating. They could not sell their crop and potatoes were dumped almost anywhere to get them out of the way. This year potato prices are up and so are carrot prices. Next year anything could happen with any number of farm products. We do not know what is going to happen and that is bad for the producer and the consumer.
It seems, Mr. Chairman, that the market in food and food products jumps from one extreme to the other from year to year. It either hits the bottom or the top, rising and falling, sometimes out of control. It is no wonder so many small businesses go under every year and so many small farms are taken out of production. The rate of failure among small businesses and small farm operations is increasing every year.
December 9, 1980

It should be mentioned here that it is not only the farms, or the producers which are decreasing in number. It is happening across the whole spectrum of the food chain. There are fewer producers, fewer wholesalers, fewer processors and fewer retailers. I believe a case can be made that control of the food industry in every sector is being concentrated in too few hands. About a month ago the Toronto Star reported that Canada suffered a deficit in foreign trade in manufactured food of $245 million in 1979 compared with a $50 million surplus in 1971. Why was it not the other way around, considering that the Canadian dollar is depressed, and our products should have been highly competitive in the world markets?
There is something seriously wrong when we cannot even take advantage of a greatly depressed dollar to sell Canadian processed food products to a hungry world. I would have thought that our products would have been in demand, but apparently that is not the case.
Perhaps this might be a good time for us to look into the question of trying to get a larger share of the foreign cheese market. There was a time when Canadian cheddar cheese was in great demand. I would like to see some energetic, imaginative and aggressive initiatives taken so as to get back into the world market in a big way.
While we are at it, Mr. Chairman, perhaps we should also consider stepping up our public relations with the consumer and producer. The federal government should take a lesson from the Ontario government and provide more useful information for the Canadian consumer. There should be more information published by the government on all aspects of the food industry, from the producer to the processor to the wholesaler. Not enough is known by the consumer about what happens to a product when it leaves the farm and moves down the chain, to the table. Good public relations and good information can remove many misconceptions from the mind of the consumer, and that would only be proper, because it is the consumer who pays the bills.
Mr. Chairman, I was interested in an article which appeared in one of the leading newspapers. This article, datelined Jordan Station, appeared in the Toronto Star on October 16, 1980, and begins as follows:
The price of an egg quota has gone past $17.55 a bird and is heading toward $20 in Ontario, according to testimony before the Ontario Farm Products Appeal Tribunal here Wednesday.
Mrs. Cornelius Super of Tavistock testified that a bid of $17.55 a bird to buy quota from a Seaforth area egg farmer was turned down in September. She and her husband bid $ 150,000 for an egg quota of 8,546 birds.
The farmer countered by offering the quota for $20 a bird, she said, while stipulating that the bird cages would go with the deal.
But Mrs. Super testified that taking the cages would have represented a cost rather than a benefit because they were in such poor shape that 'the man wanted to get them out of there, I guess.'
Selling the cages with the birds might give the farmer some tax benefits because taxes on the sale of quota might be higher than on the sale of cages. The official sales price reported to the egg board, which must approve all quota transfers, could also be lowered.
The egg board has claimed that the going price of quota, as reported to it When transfer applications come in, is running about $10 to $12 a bird.
Supply
It is articles like this appearing in our leading newspapers that make the consumer very suspicious. Eggs sell in chain-stores today for approximately $1.19 per dozen. I do not say that' is an unfair price; in fact, it is a reasonably fair price. But what would the consumer think after reading about $17.55 being offered for a laying hen quota and $20 being asked, with the cages-which are of little value-included. This is something that our agriculture industry must be concerned about. The price of the commodity must be presented fairly and I do not think an article such as this does so.
Many things are done by the Department of Agriculture that I think are beneficial to both the producer and the consumer, but there ought to be a little guidance-not too much, mind you-and a little forecasting by the department about what the future may be. We need a cushion to carry us over the lows and highs. That can apply both ways, of course.
These are some of the things the retailer is complaining about today, Mr. Chairman. I think the cost of the consumer's food basket today is a reasonably fair one but I also think much more could be done for the Canadian consumer by the food industry.

Mr. Chairman, may I say in reply to the hon. member's remarks about egg quota prices that quotas on every commodity, are under the authority of the provinces. The hon. member suggested we take a lesson from the Ontario government. I should like to tell him that we do not follow their advice. It is the Ontario government that allows quota prices to become so unrealistic. No two provinces run quotas in the same way; in fact, some of them put no value on quota at all and only redistribute quotas when a farmer sells out.
The hon. member used the price of grade A large eggs as a reference. The average price of all grades of eggs in Canada today, in 1980, is less than $1 per dozen. Not many countries in the world can make such a claim and have such a healthy egg producing industry as we have. Not one penny of tax money has been put in the egg producers' pockets since the scheme started eight years ago.
1 wonder if the hon. member could bring to my attention the case of even one egg producer who has gone bankrupt. Egg producers in Canada are the most efficient in the world. The feeding formula used to call for over eight pounds of feed to produce one dozen eggs but today a dozen eggs can be produced with less than four pounds of feed. The efficiency of the egg producing industry is the most startling in all agriculture.
The mortality rate used to be 25 per cent or higher, per year. At the present time it is .5 per cent in a laying flock. That is phenomenal, Mr. Chairman.
The hon. member also mentioned dairy farmers. Today there are 50 per cent fewer dairy farmers in Canada than there were 12 or 15 years ago. There are one-third less cattle, but more milk of a higher quality is being produced than 12 or 15 years ago. This efficiency is the envy of the world.
A rumour has been going around to the effect that the dairy farmers' quota is to be cut back. I do not know where that has
